app.name: FitLife Guide
app.disclaimer: This app provides educational information and estimates. It is not a substitute for medical diagnosis, treatment, or individualized advice from a qualified healthcare professional.
app.medicalCaution: If you are pregnant, or live with diabetes, kidney disease, an eating disorder, severe obesity, unexplained weight loss, or another chronic condition, do not use this app as treatment. Speak with a qualified healthcare professional.

sources.title: Sources & Methodology
education.title: Nutrition & fitness education
edu.protein.title: What is protein?
edu.protein.simple: Protein is a nutrient made of amino acids. The body uses it to build and repair tissues, including muscle.
edu.protein.why: Protein-containing foods can help meet everyday eating patterns. Needs vary by age, body size, and health.
edu.protein.foods: Examples in this app’s verified seed include eggs, chicken, lentils, chickpeas, mung beans, yogurt, fish, peanuts, and almonds. Values are shown only when a source record exists.
edu.protein.evidence: Nutrient values come from USDA FoodData Central SR Legacy. This is educational, not a treatment plan.
edu.carbohydrates.title: What are carbohydrates?
edu.carbohydrates.simple: Carbohydrates are a source of energy found in grains, millets, fruits, vegetables, and pulses.
edu.carbohydrates.why: Carbohydrate-containing foods also often provide fiber, and some provide vitamins and minerals.
edu.carbohydrates.foods: Rice, wheat flour, millet, fruits, and cooked pulses in the seed database.
edu.carbohydrates.evidence: USDA SR Legacy per 100 g records. Raw and cooked foods are kept as separate records.
edu.fat.title: What is fat?
edu.fat.simple: Dietary fat is a concentrated energy source and carries fat-soluble vitamins.
edu.fat.why: Different foods contain different amounts of fat. Oils are almost entirely fat.
edu.fat.foods: Olive oil, peanut oil, butter oil, nuts, egg, salmon, and whole milk in the seed database.
edu.fat.evidence: USDA SR Legacy. This app does not rank oils as medically superior.
edu.fiber.title: What is fiber?
edu.fiber.simple: Fiber is the part of plant foods that is not fully digested.
edu.fiber.why: Fiber-containing foods such as vegetables, fruits, pulses, and whole grains are part of many healthy eating patterns.
edu.fiber.foods: Guava, apple, beans, lentils, whole-wheat flour, and millets where values exist.
edu.fiber.evidence: USDA SR Legacy nutrient “Fiber, total dietary”.
edu.vitamins.title: What are vitamins?
edu.vitamins.simple: Vitamins are nutrients needed in small amounts. This app shows values only when the source record includes them.
edu.vitamins.why: Different foods contribute different vitamins. A missing value means the source did not report it here, not that the food contains zero.
edu.vitamins.foods: Fruits and vegetables often contribute vitamin C; some animal foods contribute vitamin B12.
edu.vitamins.evidence: USDA SR Legacy vitamin fields. Null means unavailable, not invented as zero.
edu.minerals.title: What are minerals?
edu.minerals.simple: Minerals such as iron, calcium, potassium, and zinc are nutrients reported in food composition tables.
edu.minerals.why: Mineral content depends on the food and on the laboratory method used by the source database.
edu.minerals.foods: Leafy vegetables, pulses, dairy, and nuts in the seed, each with its own source line.
edu.minerals.evidence: USDA SR Legacy mineral fields. Indian millet mineral values are not invented.
edu.calories.title: What are calories?
edu.calories.simple: A kilocalorie (shown as kcal) is a unit of energy. Food energy values in this app come from the source database.
edu.calories.why: Energy needs vary. Estimated BMR and TDEE are calculations, not measured metabolism.
edu.calories.foods: Every verified food shows energy per 100 g when the USDA record includes it.
edu.calories.evidence: USDA nutrient 1008 (Energy, kcal). Human energy requirement concepts: FAO/WHO/UNU 2004.
edu.bmr.title: What is BMR?
edu.bmr.simple: Basal metabolic rate is an estimate of energy used at rest. This app uses the Mifflin-St Jeor equation and labels it Estimated BMR.
edu.bmr.why: It is a starting point for estimated daily energy, not an exact measurement.
edu.bmr.foods: BMR is calculated from body size, age, and sex, not from a food.
edu.bmr.evidence: Mifflin et al., American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 1990;51(2):241-247.
edu.tdee.title: What is TDEE?
edu.tdee.simple: Estimated daily energy requirement is Estimated BMR multiplied by an activity factor.
edu.tdee.why: It is not medically exact. Activity factors are commonly used estimates.
edu.tdee.foods: TDEE is not a food nutrient.
edu.tdee.evidence: TDEE = BMR × activity factor. FAO/WHO/UNU 2004 discusses PAL ranges; this app uses the five requested multipliers.
edu.bmi.title: What is BMI?
edu.bmi.simple: BMI = weight (kg) / height (m)². For adults, WHO categories are used as a screening tool.
edu.bmi.why: BMI does not measure body fat. It is not a diagnosis.
edu.bmi.foods: BMI is not a food measure.
edu.bmi.evidence: WHO Technical Report Series 894 (2000). Child BMI is not given an adult category.
edu.metabolic.title: What is metabolic health?
edu.metabolic.simple: Metabolic health is a broad idea that includes how the body handles energy, activity, and related clinical measures that only a clinician can interpret.
edu.metabolic.why: This app does not diagnose metabolic syndrome or disease.
edu.metabolic.foods: No food is presented as a cure.
edu.metabolic.evidence: Educational framing only. Seek clinical care for blood tests or diagnosis.
edu.fitness.title: What is physical fitness?
edu.fitness.simple: Physical fitness includes aerobic capacity, strength, flexibility, and balance. This app estimates a profile only from the measures you enter.
edu.fitness.why: It is not a clinical fitness age and is not based on BMI alone.
edu.fitness.foods: Fitness is not calculated from food.
edu.fitness.evidence: WHO 2020 physical activity guidelines inform the activity targets shown.
edu.aerobic.title: What is aerobic fitness?
edu.aerobic.simple: Aerobic activity uses large muscle groups over time, such as walking, cycling, or swimming.
edu.aerobic.why: WHO 2020 recommends 150–300 moderate minutes per week for adults, or an equivalent mix.
edu.aerobic.evidence: WHO Guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour, 2020.
edu.strength.title: What is strength?
edu.strength.simple: Strength-training is activity that works major muscle groups against resistance.
edu.strength.why: WHO 2020 recommends muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days per week for adults.
edu.strength.foods: Protein foods are shown separately and are not a prescription.
edu.flexibility.title: What is flexibility?
edu.flexibility.simple: Flexibility is the range of motion around joints. Stretching and mobility work can be logged as activity.
edu.flexibility.why: This app uses an optional self-score. It is not a clinical joint exam.
edu.flexibility.evidence: Educational description. MET for stretching from the 2011 Compendium.
edu.balance.title: What is balance?
edu.balance.simple: Balance is the ability to control body position. It is especially relevant for many older adults.
edu.balance.why: WHO 2020 includes multicomponent activity for older adults. This app does not test fall risk.

plan.title: Goal plan
plan.purpose: This screen uses your body numbers and goal to estimate energy need, a cautious timeline, and foods from the verified catalog. It does not prescribe a medical diet.
plan.whatToEat: Foods that often fit this goal
plan.suggestIntro: These are verified catalog foods, not a meal prescription. Homemade recipes vary. Open a food to see the source and scale the amount.
plan.status.need_profile: Add your current weight to start a goal plan.
plan.status.need_target: Add a target weight so the app can estimate a timeline.
plan.status.need_energy: Add age, sex, height and weight so estimated BMR and daily energy can be calculated.
plan.status.target_mismatch: The target weight does not match this goal. For weight loss, target should be lower than current weight. For weight gain, it should be higher.
plan.status.already_at_target: Current weight is already near the target. Use maintenance tracking, or set a new target.
home.commonFoodsHint: Tap a food to see official per 100 g values, then log the approximate cooked weight in Diary.
diary.howTo: Choose the meal, pick the food, then enter the approximate cooked weight. The app scales official per 100 g values. It does not invent missing numbers.
coach.energy.unknown: Log foods with verified values to compare energy with your estimated target.
coach.energy.onTrack: Logged energy is near the estimated daily target. This is information, not a grade.
coach.energy.under: Logged energy is below the estimated daily target so far. That may be incomplete logging, or a lighter day.
coach.energy.over: Logged energy is above the estimated daily target. That is information for the next meal, not a failure.
coach.protein.unknown: Protein comparison appears after you log verified foods.
coach.protein.enough: Logged protein is near or above the educational 0.83 g/kg comparison.
coach.protein.under: Logged protein is below the educational 0.83 g/kg comparison so far.
coach.next.logMore: Keep logging meals so the comparison becomes clearer.
coach.next.logFoods: Start with what you ate: idli, dosa, rice, dal, chutney, or another catalog food.
coach.next.lossOver: For a weight-loss goal, the next meal can be a lower-energy verified food such as dal, yogurt, fruit, or vegetables. This is education, not a ban.
coach.next.gainUnder: For a weight-gain goal, the next meal can include a higher-energy verified food such as rice, roti, yogurt, nuts, or dal.
coach.next.keepPattern: If this matches a usual day, keep the pattern and watch the weekly weight trend, not one day.
suggest.balanced: A verified food often used in everyday meals.
suggest.lossLight: Lower energy per 100 g in the verified catalog.
suggest.lossProtein: More protein relative to energy in the verified catalog.
suggest.gainProtein: Higher energy with useful protein in the verified catalog.
suggest.gainEnergy: Higher energy per 100 g in the verified catalog.
diary.commonHint.breakfast: Common breakfast items. Sambar, pongal, lemon rice, and kurma are listed for search; they have no invented calories.
diary.commonHint.lunch: Common lunch and dinner items. Rasam, sambar, and vegetable fry stay unverified until an official Indian table is imported.
diary.commonHint.snack: Common snacks, bakery, and packaged foods. Values are USDA survey or SR Legacy copies, not homemade recipes.
plan.dayListIntro: The estimated timeline is {{days}} days. This is an educational repeating weekly pattern scaled toward your estimated daily energy. It is not a medical diet.
plan.sampleIntro: No weight timeline yet, so this shows a 7-day educational sample toward estimated daily energy.
plan.dayListCaution: Homemade recipes vary. Amounts are scaled from official USDA per 100 g values. Sambar, rasam, pongal, lemon rice, and korma stay unverified, so the list uses dal, rice, and vegetable curry instead.
scan.title: Scan food
scan.intro: Scan a plate photo, then confirm foods and sizes. Packaged barcodes load Open Food Facts. The camera cannot invent idli or dosa from pixels. Nutrition comes from the USDA catalog after you pick the food and size.
scan.hint: Scan the plate, or hold the camera on a packaged barcode.
scan.webFallback: Camera scanning is for the Android app. Tick the foods on the plate here, then pick Small, Medium, or Large.
scan.offCaution: Open Food Facts is a separate source from the USDA catalog. Log a USDA catalog match for diary calculations.
scan.noMatch: No catalog match yet. Try idli, rice, dal, or another food name.
scan.barcodeUnknown: This barcode was not found in Open Food Facts. Search the USDA catalog below.
scan.networkError: Could not reach Open Food Facts. Search the USDA catalog below.
scan.plateIntro: Take a photo of the plate. Then tick the foods you see (example: idli, vada, sambar). Pick Small, Medium, or Large for each. Nutrition is scaled from official USDA catalog values. The camera does not invent names or calories from the photo.
scan.captureFirst: Scan the plate first. After the photo, tick idli, vada, sambar, or other foods and pick a size for each.
scan.captureError: Could not take the photo. Try again.
scan.plateItemsHint: The camera cannot invent names from the photo. Tick the items on the plate, then pick Small, Medium, or Large.
scan.pickSizeHint: Pick one size to see USDA values for that amount. Sambar small is 100 g.
scan.needSizes: Select a size for each food to see the plate total.
scan.standIn.sambar: Homemade sambar has no USDA record. These numbers are USDA lentil curry (111 kcal / 100 g). Homemade sambar varies.
scan.standIn.rasam: Homemade rasam has no USDA record. These numbers are USDA lentil curry as a stand-in. Homemade rasam varies.
scan.standIn.korma: Vegetable korma has no USDA record. These numbers are USDA vegetable curry as a stand-in.
scan.standIn.fry: Vegetable fry has no USDA record. These numbers are USDA mixed vegetables, cooked, as a stand-in.
diary.nonVegList: Chicken, mutton, fish, prawns, and eggs
diary.nonVegHint: Pick a non-veg item, then choose the cooked weight. Values are USDA copies, not homemade recipes.
diary.dietHint: Switch here if today's meal is veg or non-veg. This also updates Goal and Scan lists.
